catalog_quote: in Deori, the right-most foot constitutes the metrical head of the word and rightward parsing is the optimal foot parsing in Deori. ... tone_statements.citation: Acharyya, Prarthana & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2018. Production and perception of lexical tone in Deori. In Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 18-20 June 2018, 93-97. ISCA. DOI 10.21437/TAL.2018-19.
tone_statements.quote: We have shown that Deori still has some tonal properties, marginal as they may be, which still contribute to maintaining contrast in the small sample size taken up for study in this paper. [...] Tonoexodus or tone loss in Deori is, nonetheless, reflected in the disyllable being the site of the tone target where the TBU is the entire disyllable. The loss of tonal contrast is also related to the development of an iambic system of stress. [...] It may be conjectured that Deori is in an intermediate stage where tonoexodus is not complete, but the language is on its path towards emerging as a stress-accent system without tone.

tone_statements.citation: Mahanta, Shakuntala, Indranil Dutta & Prarthana Acharyya. 2017. Lexical tone in Deori: loss, contrast and word based alignment. Papers in Historical Phonology 2: 51-87. DOI 10.2218/pihph.2.2017.1906.
tone_statements.quote: Time-normalized pitch of different words shows that words may have a lexically specified high or low tone. A high tone may contrast with a low tone, but its phonetic implementation of rise or fall in a disyllabic word depends on whether the syllable on which the contrast appears is initial or final. ... A high or a low tone may also contrast with a word which is not specified with any tone, in which case there is no rise or fall.
tone_statements.summary: Acoustic study (10 speakers): words carry a lexically specified high or low tone, or are tonally unspecified (no rise/fall); rise/fall contours are phonetic, depending on whether the contrast sits on the first or second syllable of a disyllable. No TBU statement, nothing on stress, no example forms.

sources.note: Background sketch p.66: 'The Deori phonology has allowed seventeen consonants and five vowels at segmental level. At tonal level, two tones have been recognized.' (no source or data given for the tone count). The body compares Grierson 1903 LSI forms with the author's 2008-09 field data and treats segmental/lexical changes only (lexical shift, epenthesis, devoicing, de-aspiration, vowel raising/lowering, nasalisation, elision of 'unstressed sounds', deletion, degemination, borrowing); tone, tone loss and stress placement are not analysed. Tone relevance is limited to that one sentence.

sources.citation: Nath, Arup Kumar. 2012. Sound change in Deori: a descriptive account. Journal of Universal Language 13(2): 65-89. DOI 10.22425/jul.2012.13.2.65.
sources.note: Production experiment with younger-generation speakers testing the minimal (remnant) lexical tone contrast found among older speakers, followed by a perception test; production shows a trend of underlying tone reversal (H realised with low f0, L with high: 'tone swap') in monosyllables and considerable f0 variation in disyllabic stems; listeners, mainly younger speakers, misidentify tones in monosyllables; language experience affects tone categorisation - i.e. further evidence of ongoing tone loss.

tone.n_tones: 2 (H, L) remnant contrast, unstable across generations (abstract)
